To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
liquid crystalline assemblies of GdF(₃) nanoplates can be formed at the interface between a subphase of varying composition, and that the resulting structures are characterized by SAXS.

liquid crystalline superlattices can be formed from GdF3 nanoplates by liquid interfacial self-assembly, and that the macroscopic orientation of these assemblies can be controlled by varying the subphase.

the liquid interfacial self-assembly of nanoplate building blocks can produce liquid crystalline superlattices, and the structure of the superlattices can be controlled by the subphases on which assembly occurs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the synthesis and characterization of novel nanomaterials with applications in the field of energy conversion and storage.
the synthesis and characterization of colloidal nanoscale materials, and their assembly into ordered structures.
the development and characterization of liquid crystalline superlattices of GdF(₃) nanoplates, with a particular focus on their structure, optical properties and the effect of doping with Eu(3+).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the self-assembly of Eu(3+) doped GdF(₃) nanoplates into liquid crystals with long-range positional and orientational order is demonstrated.

the liquid interfacial directed assembly of GdF(₃) nanoplates into liquid crystal superlattices can be achieved and controlled by the choice of subphase and that these superlattics can be doped with Eu(3+) to produce luminescent superlattics.

we have demonstrated that liquid crystal self-assembly can be used to produce ordered arrays of nanocrystals with controlled structure, composition and orientation, which are useful for a range of applications.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have demonstrated a new route to the preparation of luminescent liquid crystalline assemblies of nanocrystals with long range positional and orientational order.

we have demonstrated that GdF(₃) nanoplates self-assemble into a liquid crystalline phase at the air-water interface and that this assembly can be controlled by changing the composition of the subphases.
we demonstrate the liquid crystal-like self-assembly of nanoplates and the use of luminescent dopants to probe the structure and optical properties of these self-assemblies.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the combination of in situ SAXS and TEM can be used for the structural characterization of liquid crystalline superlattices.
the combination of TEM and SAXS is a powerful tool for characterizing the structure of superlattice formed from anisotropic nanoplates.
